newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-NEW FEDERAL LAW COULD RESTRICT TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-NEW FEDERAL LAW COULD RESTRICT TYSON.

text.p: A new federal law on boxing that could effectively ban Mike Tyson from fighting anywhere else in the United States if he is banned from boxing in Nevada coincidentally became official on Tuesday.
A provision of the Professional Boxing Safety Act, which was adopted by Congress last year, recommends that every state honour suspensions and bans issued by the boxing commission of any other state.
Although the law does not force states to recognise bans from other states, its authors believe states will do so to avoid public embarrassment.
If a state was unwilling to honour another state's suspension, it would have to give a written explanation to boxing officials in the state where the fighter was banned.

The law came into effect on the very day the Nevada State Athletic Commission held an emergency meeting to discuss punishing Tyson for twice biting Evander Holyfield in their World Boxing Association heavyweight title fight Saturday.

The commission scheduled a disciplinary hearing for next week, at which it could heavily fine and/or suspend Tyson for biting Holyfield's ears. Tyson was disqualified after the third round of the championship bout.

Democratic Sen. Richard Bryan, who represents Nevada in the U.S. Senate, co-sponsored the bill in an effort to prevent journeymen fighters, who might be injured or even suspended elsewhere, from fighting in other states under assumed names.
"What we have done is try to establish a floor in terms of a regulatory framework for boxing," Bryan told the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

But under the new federal law, if Tyson is suspended or has his license revoked in Nevada, he could face a nationwide ban, which would block lucrative fights in Atlantic City, New Jersey, or any other boxing venue in the United States.

Explaining the intent of the law, Representative Tom Bliley, a Republican of Virginia and chairman of the House Commerce Committee, told the newspaper: "If you're suspended in one state, you're TKO'd (technically knocked-out) everywhere.
"There is a burden on the other state to come up with the rationale for not adhering to another state's suspension."
The law also requires a nationwide boxer's license, renewable every two years, pre-fight physical examinations and health insurance for injuries sustained in the ring.
